what_its_for: Lurbinectedin is a cancer medicine used to treat adults with small cell lung cancer (SCLC) that has spread or gotten worse after trying at least one other chemotherapy treatment. It works by blocking certain proteins that cancer cells need to grow and survive.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an IV infusion (through a needle placed in your vein) by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or hospital. Each infusion takes about 60 minutes. You will NOT give yourself this medicine at home. Your healthcare team will monitor you closely during and after each infusion.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight and overall health. Most patients receive one infusion every 3 weeks (on Day 1 of each 21-day cycle). Your doctor may lower your dose or delay your treatment if you have side effects. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given at a clinic or hospital, your healthcare team will help schedule your appointments. If you miss or need to reschedule an infusion, call your doctor or clinic right away. Do not try to 'make up' a missed dose on your own — let your medical team guide you on the best next step.
storage: You do not store this medicine at home. It is prepared and stored by pharmacy professionals at your treatment center. If you are given any take-home medications related to your treatment (such as anti-nausea pills), store those as directed on the label, usually at room temperature away from heat, light, and moisture, and keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice during treatment, as they can interfere with how your body processes this medicine. Tell your doctor about ALL medicines you take, including vitamins, supplements, and herbal products, because many drugs can interact with lurbinectedin. Avoid live vaccines while on this treatment unless your doctor says it is safe. Avoid becoming pregnant or fathering a child during treatment and for several months afterward, as this medicine can harm an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control as advised by your doctor.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher (a sign of serious infection), unusual bruising or bleeding, extreme tiredness or weakness, shortness of breath, chest pain, signs of liver problems (yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, severe stomach pain), severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that will not stop, or any swelling, redness, or pain at the infusion site. These could be signs of serious side effects that need immediate attention.
when_it_works: Every patient is different. Some people may see results within a few weeks to a couple of months, but it may take longer for others. Your doctor will do regular tests (such as scans and blood work) to check how well the treatment is working. Keep all your follow-up appointments so your team can track your progress.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: This medicine can harm an unborn baby. Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant. Women who could become pregnant and men with female partners who could become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine and for at least 3 months after the last dose. Liver or Kidney Problems: If you have liver or kidney problems, your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely. Older Adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects, so extra monitoring may be needed. Always tell your entire healthcare team about all your health conditions before starting treatment.
